data.title: Flip-Flop Plinko
data.statement:
A stack of balls hangs over a board of pegs. The stack line holds a single digit: its position is the <<drop column>>, its value [[N]] is the <<number of balls>> that fall from there, one at a time. On the board, each cell is empty ({{.}}) or holds a peg ({{<}} or {{>}}).

Columns are numbered from {{0}}.

A ball falls through the rows from top to bottom. On each row, the cell in the ball's column decides the move:
{{.}} the ball keeps its column
{{<}} the ball moves one column left, and the peg becomes {{>}}
{{>}} the ball moves one column right, and the peg becomes {{<}}
The ball then falls immediately to the next row, regardless of whether its column changes or not. Its movement is not affected by another peg in the same row. Below the last row, it exits the board.

<<Flipped pegs stay flipped: subsequent balls fall through the modified board.>>

For each ball, print its exit column.

<<Example:>> 3 balls dropped into column 2. Each drawing shows the board just before that ball is dropped ({{v}} = drop column, {{^}} = exit column):
` ball 1     ball 2     ball 3
   v          v          v
 .>...      .>...      .>...
 ..<..      ..>..      ..<..
 .>...      .<...      .<...
   ^           ^       ^
   2           3       0`
Ball 1 flipped two pegs and exited down column 2. Ball 2 flipped one peg and exited down column 3. Ball 3 flipped two pegs and exited down column 0.
data.constraints:
1 ≤ [[H]] ≤ 20
1 ≤ [[N]] ≤ 9
The stack line and all board rows have the same length [[W]], with 3 ≤ [[W]] ≤ 30.
There is never a peg in the first or last column: a ball can never leave the board sideways.

lastVersion.statementHTML:
Goal

A stack of balls hangs over a board of pegs. The stack line holds a single digit: its position is the drop column, its value N is the number of balls that fall from there, one at a time. On the board, each cell is empty (.) or holds a peg (< or >).

Columns are numbered from 0.

A ball falls through the rows from top to bottom. On each row, the cell in the ball's column decides the move:
. the ball keeps its column
< the ball moves one column left, and the peg becomes >
> the ball moves one column right, and the peg becomes <
The ball then falls immediately to the next row, regardless of whether its column changes or not. Its movement is not affected by another peg in the same row. Below the last row, it exits the board.

Flipped pegs stay flipped: subsequent balls fall through the modified board.

For each ball, print its exit column.

Example: 3 balls dropped into column 2. Each drawing shows the board just before that ball is dropped (v = drop column, ^ = exit column):
 ball 1     ball 2     ball 3
   v          v          v
 .>...      .>...      .>...
 ..<..      ..>..      ..<..
 .>...      .<...      .<...
   ^           ^       ^
   2           3       0

Ball 1 flipped two pegs and exited down column 2. Ball 2 flipped one peg and exited down column 3. Ball 3 flipped two pegs and exited down column 0.
Input
Line 1: An integer H for the height of the board.
Line 2: A string for the stack line: one digit N in the drop column, . everywhere else.
Next H lines: One row of the board, containing ., < and >.
Output
N lines: An integer for the exit column of each ball on its own line, in the order they are dropped.
Constraints
1 ≤ H ≤ 20
1 ≤ N ≤ 9
The stack line and all board rows have the same length W, with 3 ≤ W ≤ 30.
There is never a peg in the first or last column: a ball can never leave the board sideways.
Example
Input
3
..3..
.>...
..<..
.>...
Output
2
3
0
